In ASCII and Unicode character sets (ASCII is a valid subset of Unicode), these non-printable characters have valid defined numeric values (binary at the level of executable computer code) just as do the visible characters.

A human reader of text containing these modified words would still see the words as they usually do (so long as a control characters like carriage return, tab, newline, form feed are not used). But a computer program would see all these characters when it's breaking the text into isolated words and these words that have hidden embedded characters would not match on their defined set of Wrong Think keywords.

Now how would we implement this? Well, at the simplest, a software program would be written that would take a text body (say its your tweet, Facebook posting, or Reddit posting that you've composed in a text editor), it would go through and analyze the text looking for keywords, when it sees a recognized keyword it would modify it by putting embedded non-printable characters into it. It would insert these hidden characters at a different position in the keyword (on each occurance) based on a random number generator. That way a keyword doesn't get modifed in an identical manner each time. The keywords would be a glossary of terms that you, yourself could define as likely to be caught as Wrong Think words by the social media Orwellian censors. These "Wrong Think" words would be put into a dictionary file that this hypothetical software program would reference.

Where does the output of this program go to? Well, it could write it to a file, but perhaps more useful would be if it would put the modified text that is the output of the program, directly into a clipboard buffer. Then all you the user have to do is go do a paste of the clipboard contents into your tweet, your Facebook posting, or Reddit posting. Then submit or publish posting.

Now take note, that each time you run this hypothetical program on the very same input text body, the detected "Wrong Think" keywords that it modifies, will be modified at a different position due to a random number generator that the program uses.
